title: CSV to GeoJSON Converter: Points as Features
description: Convert a coordinate CSV into GeoJSON points with the CSV to GeoJSON Converter — properties carried across, browser-local. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, five city rows become five GeoJSON Point features — New York at [−74.0060, 40.7128] — with name kept as a property on every feature.
quick_answer: The CSV to GeoJSON Converter turns a spreadsheet of coordinates into a GeoJSON FeatureCollection of points, carrying the other columns across as properties. Paste a clean CSV and download web-map-ready geography: the format Leaflet, MapLibre, QGIS and every geo API already speak, produced in your browser.

so only good rows become features.
QGIS and friends ingest GeoJSON natively. Converting once beats fighting CSV dialect settings in every project.
GeoJSON is the interchange dialect of geo APIs and PostGIS loaders. A clean FeatureCollection is the deliverable they all accept.
Email a file, not a screenshot: recipients open features with properties intact, ready to map their own way.

examples.label: Example · Anatomy of one converted row

body.t: The row ‘New York,40.7128,-74.0060’ becomes a Feature whose geometry is a Point at [−74.0060, 40.7128] — note the order flip: GeoJSON is longitude,latitude, always — and whose properties carry {name: ‘New York’}.

Coordinate cells become JSON numbers in the geometry; other columns ride as properties. A rating of 4.5 in your CSV is a string or a number downstream depending on the cell — worth a glance before analysis treats it as text.

popular_table.title: CSV versus GeoJSON
popular_table.note: GeoJSON coordinates are WGS84 longitude/latitude by specification (RFC 7946). Projected spreadsheet coordinates must be converted to degrees before this crossing, or the features land in the ocean off Africa.

faq: The latitude and longitude columns the file declares — matched by header. The remaining columns become the feature’s properties, names and all.
This converter mints points — one feature per row. Lines and polygons are authored as GeoJSON directly or built in GIS from ordered points.
Rows without valid coordinates cannot become points. Validate first; converting a dirty file and hunting missing features afterwards is the slow path.
Browser conversion handles ordinary datasets — thousands to tens of thousands of rows. Beyond that, command-line tools (ogr2ogr) wear the same conversion at scale.
Text stays text; coordinate cells become numbers. If a property must be numeric downstream, check its cells carry no units or text.
GeoJSON to CSV is a flattening (points only, properties to columns) — other tools here and in GIS do it; geometry beyond points has no honest CSV shape.
Standard comma CSV with quoted fields honoured. Semicolon exports should be re-exported or converted to commas first.
